analysis.title: Stablecoin growth – opportunity or threat for banks?
key_insights: ING's Marine Leleux argues broad stablecoin adoption could affect European banks through funding, credit provision and concentration risk, but banks can also benefit by issuing their own tokens. The base scenario assumes widespread adoption of euro-denominated stablecoins in Europe.
Stablecoin market capitalisation is above $300bn globally, 99% of it USD-pegged. The sector is up about $250bn over five years and is still small next to bank deposits.

If users buy EUR stablecoins with bank deposits, banks could see a net drop in retail and corporate deposits or a change in the makeup of their funding. If users redeem liquid investments instead, the impact is limited.

Under MiCAR, stablecoin issuers must hold part of their reserves as deposits at European commercial banks. Part of the outflow therefore returns as wholesale (financial institution) deposits, which shifts funding rather than shrinking it.

Wholesale deposits are more volatile than retail deposits and carry higher capital requirements, with higher LCR run-off rates and lower NSFR available stable funding weights. They are costlier for banks to hold and make asset-liability matching more complex.

Because regulation bans issuers from paying holders directly, stablecoins become attractive as a deposit substitute mainly when interest rates are very low. Falling rates could trigger a sudden adoption shift. Rising rates could trigger redemptions that force issuers to pull reserves from banks.
Banks with many digitally active customers, and deposit accounts used for payments by younger digital-native customers, face the most pressure.

If USD stablecoins keep dominating, adoption would mean a net outflow of European deposits to US issuers, which place reserves in US safe assets. European banks would need costlier alternative funding.

On credit provision, higher liquidity requirements could push banks away from illiquid, long-maturity loans, cut volumes, shorten maturities and raise loan pricing. The ECB has shown deposit substitution could contract lending to firms by about 0.2%. Banks with high loan-to-deposit ratios or close to regulatory thresholds are more likely to pass costs on.

Concentration risk rises if bank funding depends on a few stablecoin issuers, or if issuers use only a few banks. Spillover risk runs both ways: a stablecoin run could hit banks holding issuer reserves, and trouble at a reserve bank could hit issuers.

The European Commission opened a MiCAR consultation in May 2026. In September the ECB and the 27 national central banks recommended dropping the requirement to hold reserves as deposits at commercial banks, and instead requiring a minimum share of assets maturing within one to five working days.
ING notes the ESCB proposal could turn a funding shift into a net deposit outflow for banks. The Bank of England aims to ban issuers from holding reserves at commercial banks.

The current ban on issuers paying holders directly is a regulatory advantage for banks. The US CLARITY Act negotiations could allow direct rewards in 2027, which would be a first globally. Banks could respond by raising deposit rates, at a cost to profitability.

Banks' main competitive response is innovation: instant payments and deposit tokenisation, which offers faster settlement, 24/7 transactions and programmability while staying within the existing supervisory framework.
Banks can also issue their own stablecoins to keep client relationships and avoid becoming commodity providers. Bank-issued EUR stablecoins could support EU strategic autonomy in payments.

Regulatory calendar: the EU MiCAR review could change the reserve framework, the UK enforces its stablecoin regime in October 2027, and the US must still finalise the CLARITY Act. ING concludes banks are unlikely to surrender ground to fintech issuers without a fight.

sector_views.rationale: Stablecoin adoption poses funding, credit and concentration risks, but banks have tools to counter them and can benefit by issuing tokens. ING expects banks to compete rather than cede ground.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Still small next to bank deposits, but growth of about $250bn over five years has drawn regulatory attention.

macro_indicators.indicator: ECB estimate of lending to firms under deposit substitution
macro_indicators.interpretation: Deposit substitution toward stablecoins could modestly reduce bank lending to firms.

crypto_views: Stablecoin market cap is above $300bn and 99% USD-pegged. Chart sources list USDT (Tether), USDC (Circle) and USDS (Sky Protocol) as the selected stablecoins.
Allowing issuers to pay rewards directly under the US CLARITY Act would let stablecoins serve as a store of value as well as a payment tool, and would be a world first.

Broad adoption depends on regulation, integration into payment systems and attractiveness versus other payment rails. Stablecoins remain far from widespread adoption and are used mainly within crypto and by digitally savvy users.
risk_factors: Retail deposits shifting to wholesale funding, which is more volatile and costlier under LCR and NSFR rules.
Sudden deposit flows driven by interest rates: adoption at very low rates, redemptions at higher rates.
Net deposit outflow from Europe to US issuers if USD stablecoins dominate.
Credit contraction and higher loan pricing, especially at banks with high loan-to-deposit ratios.
Concentration of bank funding in a few stablecoin issuers, and spillover from a stablecoin run to banks holding reserves.
Regulatory change that could raise the impact on banks, such as the ESCB proposal to drop the bank-deposit reserve requirement.
US rule change allowing issuers to pay rewards, which could force banks to raise deposit rates and reduce profitability.
geopolitical: EU strategic autonomy agenda and reliance on non-EU, mainly US-based, payment services, with bank-issued EUR stablecoins proposed as a European alternative.
Diverging stablecoin regulation across the EU (MiCAR review), the UK (Bank of England reserve restrictions, regime enforced October 2027) and the US (CLARITY Act).

tension_points.bull_case: Banks can counter stablecoins through instant payments, deposit tokenisation and their own bank-issued stablecoins, which would keep client relationships and add fee revenue. Under MiCAR, part of any deposit outflow returns as issuer reserve deposits.
tension_points.bear_case: Deposits could shift from retail to wholesale funding, which is more volatile and costlier under LCR and NSFR. Credit provision could contract, and concentration and spillover risks could rise. The ESCB proposal to drop the bank-deposit reserve requirement could turn a funding shift into a net outflow.
tension_points.what_invalidates: US CLARITY Act approval allowing issuers to pay rewards directly, or an EU MiCAR change removing the bank-deposit reserve requirement, would worsen the outlook for banks.

theme_stances.key_argument: Broad stablecoin adoption could shift or reduce bank funding and credit provision, but banks have tools to compete and are unlikely to cede ground to fintech issuers.
theme_stances.evidence: banks to surrender ground to fintech stablecoin issuers without a fight
